title: Horizons: Delivery
tagline: The Delivery Horizon, then practice and competencies to close the series (Ch 7–9).

caseStudy.title: Delivered right first time: last-mile reliability
caseStudy.summary: Southern Cross Freight is a fictional national parcel and freight carrier moving around 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% of consignments arrive within their promised delivery window, 9% fail at the first delivery attempt, and receivers and shippers chase status through the contact centre. The target outcome is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better within 12 months, with 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%. Across the three days we follow this one idea from investment decision (Strategy), through a funded initiative and product (Initiative), to a single elaborated backlog item (Delivery).
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

participant.bigIdea: Delivery is where hypotheses meet reality — in days, not quarters.
participant.overview:
We recap Day 2 — product vision, impact map and ordered features with hypotheses — and cross into the Delivery Horizon. For the running case, the top feature is **receiver delivery-window confirmation**: the evening before delivery, the receiver is asked directly to confirm they'll be in or choose a safe drop, rather than the driver finding out at the door. Today that feature becomes a backlog item that's genuinely ready, built and measured.

New to the series? You'll get the horizons model and the case in the next few minutes. Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

sections.heading: What changes at Delivery
sections.body: The time frame shrinks to an iteration (often one to two weeks) or a continuous flow. Analysis becomes **just-in-time and just-enough**: the team needs shared understanding of the next few items, not the whole backlog. The analyst's attention shifts to conversations, examples and acceptance — while keeping one eye on the Initiative and Strategy horizons so the team doesn't optimise the wrong thing.

modules.title: The analyst at the Delivery Horizon
modules.subtitle: Inside the team: conversations, roles and shared understanding

participant.bigIdea: In a delivery team the analyst's job is shared understanding — the story card is just a reminder of a conversation.
participant.overview: At the Delivery Horizon the analyst works inside or alongside the team, helping it understand the next few backlog items well enough to build and test them. That means facilitating conversations, finding examples, clarifying rules, uncovering non-functional needs and confirming that what's built delivers the intended value. This session defines the role and who you work with; the 'ready' and 'done' boundaries come later in Planning and delivery techniques.
objectives: Describe the analyst's contribution inside a delivery team.
Use the card–conversation–confirmation idea to frame stories.
Identify who you work with at Delivery and what each needs from you.

keyPoints.title: Card, conversation, confirmation
keyPoints.body: The card names it, the conversation builds understanding, the confirmation (examples, criteria) proves it.

keyPoints.title: Done means valuable
keyPoints.body: Built, tested, accepted — and, where possible, measured.

keyPoints.title: The analyst as team member
keyPoints.body: You may test, demo, write examples or pair with developers. Titles matter less than outcomes.

sections.heading: What the analyst does at Delivery
sections.body:
1. **Refine** upcoming items with the PO and team.
2. **Split** features into thin, valuable stories.
3. **Elaborate** with examples, rules and acceptance criteria.
4. **Surface NFRs** — security, privacy, accessibility, performance.
5. **Support build and test** — answer questions fast, review increments.
6. **Validate value** — check the signal after release and feed back to the PO.

sections.heading: Card, conversation, confirmation
sections.body:
- **Card** — a short statement that names the need and reminds everyone a conversation is owed.
- **Conversation** — the analyst, product owner, developers and testers build shared understanding, usually with examples on a whiteboard.
- **Confirmation** — the agreed examples and acceptance criteria that prove the team understood the same thing.

If the card is detailed but the conversation never happened, the team has a document, not an understanding.

sections.heading: Who you work with at Delivery
sections.body:
| Role | What they need from the analyst |
|---|---|
| Product owner | Items ordered by value, with the hypothesis and signal attached |
| Developers | Rules, examples and quick answers mid-iteration |
| Testers | Examples that become test cases; edge and unhappy paths |
| UX / design | The customer's context and journey, not just the screen |
| Subject-matter experts (Legal, WHS, depot ops) | Precise questions, asked early |
| Operations / support | What will change for them at release |

sections.heading: The running case at Delivery
sections.body: For **receiver delivery-window confirmation**, the analyst would confirm with Legal what the SMS may contain and what consent is needed, work with a depot route planner on when the window must be confirmed (before the 5 am route lock), find examples (house with a safe porch, apartment with a concierge, small business receiver closed on Saturdays) and ensure the notice is accessible and privacy-safe — the receiver's details must not be over-shared with drivers, and safe-drop choices must not create WHS hazards for drivers.

modules.title: Outcomes · time frame · feedback
modules.subtitle: Iteration outcomes, the Delivery time frame and value metrics

participant.bigIdea: A story isn't finished when it ships — it's finished when you know whether it worked.
participant.overview: At Delivery, outcomes are working increments that move product metrics. The time frame is an iteration or continuous flow, and feedback comes from demos, tests and usage data. In this session you'll define a **value metric** for a story and link it to the feature signal and strategic outcome. (The one-week horizon calendar moves to session 3.7, where we work across horizons.)
objectives: Define delivery outcomes and value metrics.
Describe the Delivery time frame for iterative and flow-based teams.
Link a story's value metric to the feature signal and strategic outcome.

keyPoints.title: Value metric
keyPoints.body: A measure the story should move, with a baseline, expected change and how it's captured.

keyPoints.title: Fast feedback
keyPoints.body: Demo every iteration; instrument releases; review metrics within days.

keyPoints.title: Short time frame
keyPoints.body: Days to an iteration — so analysis is sized to what the team will build next.

sections.heading: Delivery outcomes and value metrics
sections.body:
| Level | Running case example |
|---|---|
| Strategic | On-time last-mile delivery ≥92% |
| Feature signal | ≥70% of receivers respond before route lock |
| Story value metric | % of notifications opened within 4 hours; % confirmed via one-click link |

A story value metric should be **observable soon after release**, **instrumented as part of done**, and **causally linked** to the feature signal.

sections.heading: Time frame at Delivery
sections.body:
| | Iteration-based team | Flow-based team |
|---|---|---|
| Planning unit | 1–2 week iteration | Next item pulled when capacity frees |
| How far ahead the analyst works | 1–2 iterations | The top of the ready queue (often 5–10 items) |
| When feedback arrives | Review at iteration end; usage data days after release | Continuously, as each item is released |
| Risk to watch | Over-refining items that slip | A ready queue that empties because analysis lags |

Either way, the rule is the same: work just far enough ahead that the team never waits, and no further.

sections.heading: Feedback in the iteration
sections.body:
- **Daily:** questions answered, examples refined.
- **Mid-iteration:** show work-in-progress to the PO.
- **End of iteration:** demo against acceptance criteria; agree what's done.
- **Post-release (days):** check the value metric; feed back to the feature hypothesis.

activities.title: Value metric for my story
activities.instructions: For your feature, pick one story and define its value metric: baseline, expected change, capture method and link to the feature signal.

prompts.label: Link to feature signal and strategic outcome

participant.aiPrompt: Help me plan a one-week calendar as a business analyst working across three horizons: Strategy (investment decisions, evidence for portfolio reviews), Initiative (product vision, impact maps, roadmaps, user research) and Delivery (refinement, examples, acceptance, demos). Given my current commitments below, propose a Monday–Friday plan with time blocks for each horizon, a suggested ratio, and one activity I should stop or delegate. My commitments:

quiz.q: A good story value metric is…
opts: Observable soon after release and linked to the feature signal
quiz.why: It should show whether the story moved the behaviour intended.

quiz.q: When is a story's value metric best instrumented?
opts: As part of the definition of done
quiz.why: Instrumenting as part of done ensures feedback actually arrives.

quiz.q: How far ahead should a Delivery analyst usually be working?
opts: Just far enough that the team never waits — often 1–2 iterations
quiz.why: Working further ahead wastes effort on items that may change or slip.

takeaways: Instrument value as part of done.
Link story → feature signal → outcome.
Work just far enough ahead — no further.

presenter.purpose: Teach delivery outcomes, the Delivery time frame and value metrics.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Value metrics feel unfamiliar to many BAs. Use the running-case table repeatedly. If someone proposes story points or velocity, ask: 'would a receiver notice?'
presenter.whatGood: A value metric with baseline, expected change, capture method and an explicit link to the feature signal.
presenter.commonFailure: Output metrics ('story delivered') — the fix: what behaviour should change, and how would we see it?
debrief: Which value metric is hardest to instrument?
Who in your team would own the post-release check?
presenter.answerKey: Running case story: 'Receiver confirms delivery window or chooses a safe drop via one-click link'. Value metric: % of notified receivers confirming within 4 hours; baseline n/a (new channel) — compare to the current first-attempt failure rate of ~9% (illustrative); capture: link click, confirmation and safe-drop events logged; links to feature signal ≥70% before route lock.

modules.title: Principles applied at this horizon
modules.subtitle: How each agile BA principle changes shape when the decision is the next slice

participant.bigIdea: The same seven principles — at Delivery they're decided in minutes, not months.
participant.overview: On Days 1 and 2 we applied the seven agile BA principles to investment and product decisions. At Delivery they shrink to the grain of a single story and a single conversation. This session walks each principle at Delivery, shows one in action through a customer-focused review, and looks at what to do when principles pull against each other inside an iteration.
objectives: Apply each of the seven principles to a Delivery decision.
Use 'think as a customer' to reframe a review or demo.
Resolve a principle conflict inside an iteration.

keyPoints.title: Get real using examples
keyPoints.body: The principle most at home at Delivery — examples become the confirmation.

keyPoints.title: Think as a customer
keyPoints.body: Demo the receiver's or driver's journey, not the screen.

keyPoints.title: Avoid waste
keyPoints.body: Just enough detail for the next item; don't refine what may never be built.

keyPoints.title: Understand what is doable
keyPoints.body: Capacity, data and legal limits decide the slice.

sections.heading: The principles at Delivery
sections.body:
| Principle | Question to ask at Delivery | Running case example |
|---|---|---|
| See the whole | Does this story still serve the feature hypothesis and the outcome? | Confirmation link only matters if the driver's run sheet updates |
| Think as a customer | What will the receiver or driver actually experience? | A link opened at 6 am after route lock |
| Analyse to determine value | Which slice moves the signal soonest? | One-click confirm before email fallback |
| Get real using examples | Which concrete cases prove we agree? | House, apartment with concierge, closed small business |
| Understand what is doable | What can this team finish this iteration? | Middleware event exists; SMS gateway contract does too |
| Stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement | Who needs to be in the conversation? | Tester and depot route planner in refinement |
| Avoid waste | What detail can wait? | Email-fallback wording until story 3 is next |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: Running case: a review that thinks as a customer
sections.body: Rather than 'here's the notification email template', demo it as Mei, a shift-working nurse waiting on a parcel: receive the notice on a Tuesday evening, see what's asked, confirm with one click. Then show the early value metric. The conversation shifts from 'does it look right?' to 'will Mei act on it?'

sections.heading: When principles conflict in an iteration
sections.body:
Mid-iteration, *get real* surfaces a new edge case (a receiver with two consignments arriving on different days). *Avoid waste* says don't expand the story. *Think as a customer* says the receiver will be confused.

Resolve it the same way as on Days 1 and 2: **which decision is next, and what does it need?** Usually the answer is to capture the case as a new example, split it into its own story, and let the product owner order it — not to quietly grow the current story.

activities.title: Principle check on my item
activities.instructions: Take your chosen feature or story. For three of the seven principles, write the Delivery question and your honest answer. Note one conflict you can see coming and how you'd resolve it.

prompts.label: A likely conflict, and my resolution

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an agile business analysis coach. For the backlog item below, ask me the Delivery-horizon question for each of the seven agile BA principles (see the whole; think as a customer; analyse to determine what is valuable; get real using examples; understand what is doable; stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement; avoid waste). Then identify which two principles are most at risk for this item and why. Backlog item:

quiz.q: Which principle is most at home in backlog refinement?
quiz.why: Refinement is where examples build shared understanding.

quiz.q: A new edge case appears mid-iteration. The best default is to…
opts: Quietly add it to the current story
Capture it as an example, split it out and let the PO order it
quiz.why: This respects avoid waste and think as a customer, and keeps ordering with the PO.

quiz.q: An iteration review that 'thinks as a customer' would…
opts: Walk the customer's journey through the increment and show the value metric
quiz.why: It focuses on the experience and value delivered.

takeaways: Same principles, smaller grain.
Demo journeys, not screens.
New cases become new examples — and often new stories.

presenter.purpose: Carry the seven principles down to Delivery and practise resolving conflicts.
presenter.openingLine: "On Day 1 'avoid waste' meant not writing a 60-page business case. Today it means not refining a story nobody will build. Same principle — smaller grain."

beats.label: Principles table
beats.notes: Walk each row; compare one row with Day 1's version.

beats.label: Customer-focused review roleplay
beats.notes: Presenter plays Mei; a volunteer plays the BA.

beats.label: Conflict example
beats.notes: Two consignments, different days.

beats.label: Principle check activity
beats.notes: Individual.

beats.notes: Collect likely conflicts in chat.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Pre-lunch energy can dip — the roleplay helps. Keep language framework-neutral (Scrum, Kanban, SAFe). Point back to the Day 1 and Day 2 principle tables for returning participants.

roleplay.line: "I got this text — is it a scam? It mentions a Southern Cross Freight delivery I didn't know about."
roleplay.curveball: "Why wasn't I told before the retailer sent it?"
roleplay.move: Show the trust cues in the notice (sender name, retailer and order reference, no request to log in or pay), and explain that the notice is designed to let receivers act before the driver arrives — then capture the trust concern as a new example for refinement.

presenter.whatGood: Concrete Delivery questions per principle, and a conflict resolved by splitting rather than expanding.
presenter.commonFailure: Restating the principle as the answer ('we'll see the whole') — the fix: what specific thing will you check, with whom?
debrief: Which principle is hardest to apply in your team?
What did the roleplay reveal about the notice design?
presenter.answerKey: Running case: see the whole — confirm the run-sheet update is in scope; get real — three receiver examples agreed with the route planner; avoid waste — defer email-fallback wording. Likely conflict: consignments split across days; resolve by a new story ordered by the PO.

modules.title: Analysis techniques
modules.subtitle: Story splitting, examples and acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements

participant.bigIdea: Thin, testable slices with real examples are the analyst's highest-leverage Delivery technique.
participant.overview: The main analysis block of Day 3. You'll split the running-case feature into stories, then elaborate one with **examples (specification by example)**, **acceptance criteria** and **non-functional requirements**. Working across horizons and at scale now has its own session (3.7).
objectives: Split a feature into thin, valuable stories using splitting patterns.
Elaborate a story with examples and Given/When/Then acceptance criteria.
Identify NFRs relevant to the story.

keyPoints.title: Split by value, not layer
keyPoints.body: Split by workflow step, rule, data variation or happy/unhappy path — never 'front end' and 'back end'.

keyPoints.title: Examples first
keyPoints.body: Agree concrete examples; criteria follow naturally.

keyPoints.title: NFRs are requirements
keyPoints.body: Privacy, security, accessibility, performance and audit belong in the story or definition of done.

sections.heading: Splitting the feature
sections.body:
Feature: **receiver delivery-window confirmation**. Possible stories:

1. Notify receiver by SMS the evening before delivery (happy path).
2. Receiver confirms the window or chooses a safe drop via one-click link.
3. Notify by email when no mobile number is on file.
4. Flag to the depot when a receiver hasn't responded by route lock.
5. Handle consignments with no receiver contact details.

Story 2 is a good first candidate: it directly drives the feature signal and is thin.

sections.heading: Elaborating with examples
sections.body:
**Story:** *As a receiver, I want to confirm my delivery window or choose a safe drop from the notification, so that my consignment arrives on the first attempt.*

| Example | Receiver | Consignment | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | House, mobile on file, home | Standard parcel | One-click confirm; driver run updated |
| 2 | House, out at work | Standard parcel | Chooses 'front porch' safe drop; instruction shown to driver |
| 3 | Small business | Two cartons | Confirm without creating an account |
| 4 | Any | Link opened after 5 am route lock | Link expired; prompted to contact us; no consignment data shown |

**Acceptance criteria:**

- *Given* a notified receiver, *when* they select Confirm, *then* the consignment is marked 'receiver confirmed' and the driver's run is updated within 5 minutes.
- *Given* the receiver chooses a safe drop, *when* they submit, *then* the instruction is recorded with the original delivery preference and shown on the driver's run sheet.
- *Given* a link opened after route lock, *when* it loads, *then* the receiver sees an expiry message and contact details, and no consignment data is shown.

sections.heading: Non-functional requirements
sections.body:
| NFR | Story-level requirement (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Privacy | Receiver sees only their own consignment and window; driver sees only the address and safe-drop instruction |
| Security | Single-use, time-limited link; no login credentials or payment requested |
| Accessibility | Page meets WCAG 2.2 AA; works on mobile |
| Performance | Confirmation page loads in <2 seconds on 4G |
| WHS | Safe-drop options never require the driver to climb, enter premises or lift over a fence; items over 25 kg are not offered safe drop |
| Audit | Every confirmation and change logged with timestamp and source |
| Trust | Notice includes retailer name, consignment reference and verifiable sender to reduce scam concerns |

**Value metric:** % of notified receivers confirming within 4 hours (target trajectory to ≥70% before route lock at feature level).

activities.title: Split the feature
activities.instructions: Split your feature into at least four stories using value-based patterns. Mark the one to elaborate first and why.

activities.title: Elaborate one story
activities.instructions: For your chosen story, write: the story statement, at least four examples (including edge cases), three Given/When/Then criteria, relevant NFRs and a value metric. You'll finish and trace it in session 3.9.

prompts.label: Story statement
prompts.placeholder: As a… I want… so that…

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an agile business analyst. For the story below: (1) propose at least five concrete examples in a table including edge cases and an unhappy path; (2) write three to five Given/When/Then acceptance criteria derived from the examples; (3) list non-functional requirements across privacy, security, accessibility, performance, audit and trust; (4) suggest a value metric that is observable within days of release and links to the feature hypothesis. Point out any ambiguity I need to resolve with the product owner or a subject-matter expert. Story and context:

quiz.q: Which is a value-based way to split a story?
opts: By business rule or data variation
quiz.why: Splitting by rule or variation keeps each slice valuable and testable.

quiz.q: In specification by example, which comes first?
opts: Concrete examples agreed with the team
quiz.why: Examples build shared understanding; criteria are distilled from them.

quiz.q: An NFR for the receiver confirmation story should include…
opts: Showing the receiver's full order history to the driver
Privacy: driver sees only the address and safe-drop instruction
Requiring the receiver to create a new account password
quiz.why: Minimising what each party sees is essential; the others are wrong or add friction.

takeaways: Split by value, not by layer.
Examples first, criteria second.
NFRs belong in the story or done.

presenter.purpose: Produce the main leave-with artefact — one story elaborated with examples, criteria, NFRs and a value metric.
presenter.openingLine: "Let's take one small piece of this and make it so clear that a developer, a tester and Mei, a shift-working nurse waiting on a parcel would all describe it the same way."

beats.label: Splitting patterns
beats.notes: Show the five stories; ask which they'd do first.

beats.label: Activity: split
beats.notes: Pairs.

beats.label: Examples, criteria and NFRs demo
beats.notes: Walk the running case story; derive criteria from examples live.

beats.label: Activity: elaborate one story
beats.notes: Pairs or trios; visit rooms at 10 and 20 minutes.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: One group shares their trickiest example.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Groups often write criteria before examples — redirect. Push for at least one unhappy path and a privacy NFR. Unfinished stories are fine: participants finish them in 3.9.
presenter.whatGood: Four or more examples incl. edge cases; criteria traceable to examples; NFRs covering privacy and accessibility; a value metric observable within days.
presenter.commonFailure: Criteria that restate the story ('the receiver can confirm') — the fix: what exact observable result, for which example?
debrief: What NFR would you normally have missed?
presenter.answerKey: Model elaboration as in sections 2–3. Additional strong examples: receiver in an apartment with a concierge; consignment split across two deliveries; a safe-drop request for a 30 kg item (rejected under the WHS rule); duplicate notification for the same consignment.

modules.title: Planning and delivery techniques
modules.subtitle: Definition of ready and done, ordering the next slice, and the analyst in each agile event

participant.bigIdea: Ready and done are conversation checklists — and agile events are where the principles either live or die.
participant.overview: Analysis techniques make an item understood; planning and delivery techniques get it built, accepted and measured. This session covers a lightweight **definition of ready and done**, how the analyst helps order the next slice and shape the iteration goal, and the analyst's contribution to each **agile event**.
objectives: Agree a lightweight definition of ready and definition of done.
Connect an iteration goal to a feature hypothesis.
Describe and upgrade the analyst's contribution to each agile event.

keyPoints.title: Ready enough
keyPoints.body: Small, valuable, understood, testable — not fully specified.

keyPoints.title: Done means valuable
keyPoints.body: Built, tested, accepted — and the value metric instrumented.

keyPoints.title: Iteration goal
keyPoints.body: One sentence that says which hypothesis this iteration tests.

keyPoints.title: Events
keyPoints.body: Refinement, planning, stand-up, review and retrospective each need something different from you.

sections.heading: Ready and done
sections.body:
| Definition of ready (lightweight) | Definition of done (example) |
|---|---|
| Traces to a feature hypothesis | Acceptance criteria pass |
| Small enough to finish in the iteration | NFRs met and verified |
| Key examples agreed | Accessibility checked (WCAG 2.2 AA) |
| Dependencies known | Privacy impact considered |
| Acceptance criteria drafted | Demonstrated to PO and accepted |
| | Value metric instrumented |

Beware turning 'ready' into a stage gate — it's a conversation checklist.

sections.heading: Ordering the next slice and the iteration goal
sections.body:
The product owner orders the backlog; the analyst makes ordering easier by putting **value, risk and learning** next to each ready item. An iteration goal then ties the work to the feature hypothesis.

*Running case iteration goal (illustrative):* 'Receivers in the two pilot depots can confirm a delivery window or safe drop from an SMS, so we can see whether ≥70% respond before route lock.'

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: The analyst in each event
sections.body:
| Event | Principle in focus | What the analyst does |
|---|---|---|
| Backlog refinement | Get real using examples | Brings examples and questions; facilitates splitting |
| Iteration planning | See the whole | Connects the iteration goal to the feature hypothesis; flags dependencies |
| Daily stand-up | Collaborate | Unblocks questions fast; spots misunderstanding early |
| Iteration review | Think as a customer | Frames the demo around the receiver's or driver's journey; shows the value metric |
| Retrospective | Continuous improvement | Raises analysis-related improvements (late NFRs, unclear examples) |

activities.title: Ready check
activities.instructions: Apply the definition of ready to your chosen feature. What's missing? Draft one sentence for each missing element.

prompts.label: Ready criteria missing, and how I'll close each gap

activities.title: Event upgrade
activities.instructions: Pick the event where you currently add least. Write what you'll do differently next time, which principle it applies, and how you'll know it helped.

participant.aiPrompt: Act as a delivery-team business analyst. For the feature below: (1) check it against this definition of ready — traces to a hypothesis; small enough for one iteration; key examples agreed; dependencies known; acceptance criteria drafted — and list what's missing; (2) draft a one-sentence iteration goal that names the hypothesis being tested; (3) suggest one thing I should do differently in refinement, planning and review. Feature:

quiz.q: A definition of ready should be treated as…
quiz.why: As a gate it creates waiting; as a checklist it improves conversations.

quiz.q: A good iteration goal…
opts: Lists every ticket in the iteration
Names the hypothesis the iteration's work will test
quiz.why: It connects the iteration's work to the outcome it's meant to move.

quiz.q: Which belongs in a definition of done at Delivery?
quiz.why: Instrumenting the value metric ensures feedback actually arrives.

takeaways: Ready is a checklist, not a gate.
Done includes instrumenting value.
Each event is a chance to apply a principle.

presenter.purpose: Teach ready/done, iteration goals and the analyst's role in agile events.
presenter.openingLine: "Show of hands: who's had a story 'signed off' that the developers understood completely differently? Let's make sure 'ready' prevents that without becoming a gate."

beats.label: Ready and done
beats.notes: Discuss gate vs checklist.

beats.label: Ready check activity
beats.notes: Individual.

beats.label: Ordering and iteration goal
beats.notes: Read the running-case goal.

beats.label: Events table
beats.notes: Walk each row; poll which event they find hardest.

beats.label: Event upgrade activity
beats.notes: Individual.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Collect commitments in chat.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Many participants have strong opinions about definition of ready — allow brief debate, then refocus on the checklist framing. Keep event language framework-neutral.
presenter.whatGood: Ready gaps with concrete closing actions; an event commitment tied to a principle and a measurable signal.
presenter.commonFailure: Treating ready as 'fully specified', or commitments like 'be more engaged' — the fix: the minimum the team needs to start; which action, in which event, next week?
debrief: What's most often missing when items reach your team?
Which event did you choose to upgrade and why?
presenter.answerKey: Running case gaps: SMS content and consent rules unconfirmed; receiver contact data quality unknown; examples not agreed; WHS limits on safe drops undefined. Close by: 30-min Legal session; data profiling of receiver contacts from pilot shippers; three examples workshop; WHS review with the depot safety lead. Strong event commitments: bring three examples per item to refinement; open review with a 2-minute journey demo; add 'late NFRs found' to the retro board.

modules.title: Working across horizons and at scale
modules.subtitle: The same techniques at every altitude, a one-week horizon calendar, and analysis with many teams

participant.bigIdea: Analysts who only work at Delivery let strategy drift — every horizon needs time on purpose.
participant.overview: Real analysts don't work at one horizon. This session shows how the techniques from all three days are the same tools at different altitudes, how to plan a week that keeps Strategy and Initiative work alive alongside delivery, and what changes when several teams build one product.
objectives: Explain how core techniques change grain across the three horizons.
Build a one-week horizon calendar balancing all three horizons.
Describe what the analyst adds when several teams work on one product.

keyPoints.title: Same techniques, different altitude
keyPoints.body: Examples, hypotheses and impact thinking work at every horizon — the grain size changes.

keyPoints.title: Horizon balance
keyPoints.body: Plan named activities for Strategy and Initiative, even one hour a week.

keyPoints.title: At scale
keyPoints.body: Shared backlog and impact map, consistent examples and data definitions, joint end-to-end reviews.

sections.heading: Techniques across horizons
sections.body:
| Technique | Strategy | Initiative | Delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Examples | Walk real consignments through options | Journey walk-throughs | Specification by example |
| Hypotheses | Investment hypothesis | Feature hypotheses | Story value metrics |
| Impact thinking | Outcome tree | Impact map | Story 'so that' |
| Visual models | Value stream | Story map | Process or state model for one flow |

sections.heading: The one-week horizon calendar
sections.body:
An illustrative week for a BA on the running case:

| | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delivery (≈60%) | Refinement; examples | Pair with tester | Answer questions; review increment | Refinement | Demo; check value metric |
| Initiative (≈30%) | — | Subcontractor driver interview | Impact map update | — | Monthly review prep |
| Strategy (≈10%) | — | — | — | Evidence pack for quarterly review (1h) | — |

Ratios vary by role; the point is that every horizon gets time on purpose.

sections.heading: Analysis at scale
sections.body:
**At scale** — several teams on one product (for example booking, notification and middleware teams) — the analyst adds: a shared product backlog and impact map, cross-team refinement for dependent items, consistent examples and data definitions, and a joint review focused on the end-to-end receiver journey rather than each team's component.

Watch for three scaled-delivery smells: each team has its own definition of 'consignment' or 'delivered'; reviews show components rather than the receiver's journey; and nobody owns the feature signal across teams. The analyst is often best placed to fix all three.

activities.title: One-week horizon calendar
activities.instructions: Draft next week's calendar. Allocate time to each horizon and name the specific activity in each slot.

prompts.label: One thing I'll stop doing to make room

participant.aiPrompt: Help me plan a one-week calendar as a business analyst working across three horizons: Strategy (investment decisions, evidence for portfolio reviews), Initiative (product vision, impact maps, roadmaps, user research) and Delivery (refinement, examples, acceptance, demos). Given my current commitments below, propose a Monday–Friday plan with time blocks for each horizon, a suggested ratio, and one activity I should stop or delegate. My commitments:

quiz.q: Why plan time for Strategy and Initiative during delivery?
opts: So the team keeps building the right thing as evidence changes
quiz.why: Higher-horizon work keeps delivery aligned with outcomes.

quiz.q: At scale, a key analyst addition is…
opts: Separate backlogs per team with no shared view
Consistent examples and data definitions across teams
quiz.why: Consistency across teams keeps the end-to-end journey coherent.

quiz.q: Which technique appears at Strategy, Initiative and Delivery with a different grain?
quiz.why: Investment hypothesis → feature hypothesis → story value metric.

takeaways: Same techniques, different grain.
Put every horizon on your calendar on purpose.
At scale, own consistency and the end-to-end journey.

presenter.purpose: Close the Delivery Horizon by connecting it back to the other two, and produce the horizon calendar.
presenter.openingLine: "Honestly: what percentage of last week did you spend on Delivery? Let's see whether that's a choice or an accident."

beats.label: Techniques across horizons
beats.notes: Walk the comparison table; link each row to Days 1 and 2.

beats.label: Horizon calendar teach
beats.notes: Show the example week.

beats.label: Activity: calendar
beats.notes: Individual; then pair to challenge ratios.

beats.label: Analysis at scale
beats.notes: Three smells; ask who has seen each.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: What did you stop doing?

presenter.facilitationNotes: Many BAs find they spend 95% on delivery. Don't moralise — the calendar makes it visible. Encourage small, specific Strategy slots (even one hour). Participants in single-team settings can treat the scale section as preparation.
presenter.whatGood: A calendar with named activities on every horizon and one thing stopped to make room.
presenter.commonFailure: Calendars with 'strategy time' as a vague block — the fix: name the artefact or meeting.
debrief: What's your current horizon ratio, honestly?
Which scaled-delivery smell have you seen?
presenter.answerKey: Strong calendars name the meeting or artefact in every slot (e.g. 'Thu 2–3 pm: evidence pack for quarterly portfolio review'). At scale for the running case: one shared definition of 'receiver confirmed' across the notification, booking and middleware teams; one joint review walking Mei's journey end to end.

modules.title: Common challenges · competencies
modules.subtitle: What gets in the way, and the competencies that get you through

participant.bigIdea: Agile analysis fails for predictable reasons — and the competencies that fix them can be deliberately developed.
participant.overview: We close the teaching content of the series with practice and people. First, the challenges analysts commonly meet in agile settings and practical responses. Then the competencies that matter most across horizons — and your **personal development map**.
objectives: Recognise common challenges for analysts in agile environments.
Choose a practical response to each challenge.
Self-assess against key agile BA competencies.
Build a personal development map with concrete actions.

keyPoints.title: Common challenges
keyPoints.body: Unclear role, delivery-only focus, documentation pressure, distributed teams, governance that expects waterfall artefacts.

keyPoints.title: Competencies
keyPoints.body: Analytical thinking, facilitation, communication, domain knowledge, product thinking, comfort with ambiguity, and responsible use of AI.

keyPoints.title: Development is a practice
keyPoints.body: Pick one or two competencies, practise deliberately, get feedback.

sections.heading: Challenges and responses
sections.body:
| Challenge | Symptom | Practical response |
|---|---|---|
| Role ambiguity | 'Do we still need a BA?' | Show value in outcomes: examples that prevented rework; signals you set up |
| Delivery-only trap | All time in refinement | Horizon calendar; protect a Strategy hour each week |
| Documentation pressure | Governance wants 80-page specs | Lean artefacts plus a traceability view; agree what's really needed |
| Distributed teams | Misunderstanding across time zones | Examples in writing; short recorded walkthroughs |
| Waterfall governance | Gates that expect full requirements | Map gate questions to horizon artefacts (lean case, impact map, ready items) |
| AI-generated drafts | Plausible but wrong content | You direct, the agent drafts; you verify every figure and rule |

sections.heading: Competencies across horizons
sections.body:
| Competency | Strategy | Initiative | Delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Analytical thinking | Assumption mapping, value models | Impact maps, prioritisation | Splitting, examples |
| Facilitation | Executive workshops | Co-design with drivers and receivers | Refinement and reviews |
| Communication | Lean cases, decision framing | Visions, roadmaps | Stories, criteria |
| Domain knowledge | Network economics, transport and WHS obligations | Customer journeys | Rules, data |
| Product thinking | Outcomes vs outputs | Hypotheses and signals | Value metrics |
| Comfort with ambiguity | Deciding with incomplete evidence | Changing the roadmap | Just-enough detail |
| Responsible AI use | Checking invented figures | Validating synthesised research | Reviewing generated criteria |

Rate yourself 1–5 on each, per horizon. Look for the lowest score on the horizon you most need.

sections.heading: Building a development map
sections.body: A personal development map has: (1) two focus competencies; (2) a target level and horizon for each; (3) three practice actions over the next 90 days; (4) a feedback source; (5) a check-in date. Example: *Facilitation at Strategy — from 2 to 3. Actions: co-facilitate the next quarterly review; run a 30-min assumption-mapping session with my PO; observe a senior colleague's executive workshop. Feedback: PO and BA lead. Check-in: 90 days.*

activities.title: Personal development map
activities.instructions: Self-assess on the competency table (1–5 per horizon). Choose two focus competencies and build your 90-day map.

prompts.label: Focus competency 1 — target, horizon, three actions
Focus competency 2 — target, horizon, three actions
Challenge I face most, and my response

participant.aiPrompt: Act as a business analysis career coach. Based on my self-assessment below across these competencies — analytical thinking, facilitation, communication, domain knowledge, product thinking, comfort with ambiguity, responsible AI use — at the Strategy, Initiative and Delivery horizons, recommend two focus competencies, explain why, and propose a 90-day development plan with three practical actions each, a feedback source and a check-in date. Keep actions achievable within my normal work. Self-assessment and context:

quiz.q: A good response to the 'delivery-only trap' is…
opts: Plan horizon time deliberately, e.g. a protected Strategy hour
Ask the PO to do strategy
quiz.why: Deliberate calendar allocation keeps higher horizons alive.

quiz.q: When using an AI agent to draft analysis, the BA should…
opts: Direct the agent and verify every figure and rule
quiz.why: The agent removes the blank page; judgement and verification stay with the BA.

quiz.q: A personal development map should include…
opts: Two focus competencies with actions, feedback and a check-in date
quiz.why: Focus and deliberate practice with feedback drive growth.

takeaways: Challenges are predictable — prepare responses.
Assess competencies per horizon.
Focus on two, practise deliberately, get feedback.

presenter.purpose: Address real-world obstacles and produce the personal development map.
presenter.openingLine: "We've spent three days on what good looks like. Now let's talk honestly about what gets in the way — and what you'll work on next."

beats.label: Challenges and responses
beats.notes: Walk the table; ask for one more challenge from the room.

beats.label: Competencies across horizons
beats.notes: Explain self-rating per horizon.

beats.label: Development map example
beats.notes: Read the example.

beats.label: Activity: development map
beats.notes: Individual; quiet time.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Two volunteers share a focus competency and first action.

presenter.facilitationNotes: This is reflective — give quiet time and don't rush. Some participants may be anxious about role security; acknowledge it and redirect to demonstrable outcomes.
presenter.whatGood: Two focus competencies with concrete actions, a feedback source and a date.
presenter.commonFailure: Development maps that are a list of courses — the fix: what will you practise in your current work?
debrief: Which challenge do you face most?
What's your first action on Monday?
presenter.answerKey: Strong maps tie actions to existing work (e.g. 'run the examples workshop for story 3 next sprint'), name a specific person for feedback and set a date.

modules.title: Exercise: elaborate one backlog item · close
modules.subtitle: Finish your story, check the thread, close the series

participant.bigIdea: One item, fully understood and measured, tells you more than a hundred specified ones.
participant.overview: Finalise the backlog item you started in session 3.5: story, examples, criteria, NFRs and value metric. Then trace it all the way back to the strategic outcome — closing the thread that started with an 18-day wait on Day 1. We finish with commitments and close the Horizon Series.
objectives: Finalise one fully elaborated backlog item.
Trace it from story to strategic outcome.
Commit to next actions from your horizon calendar and development map.

keyPoints.title: Complete the item
keyPoints.body: Story, examples, criteria, NFRs, value metric.

keyPoints.title: Trace the thread
keyPoints.body: Story → feature signal → product outcome → strategic outcome.

keyPoints.title: Commit
keyPoints.body: One action from each leave-with artefact.

sections.heading: Exercise brief
sections.body:
1. Finalise your elaborated story.
2. Write the full trace: story value metric → feature signal → product outcome → strategic outcome.
3. Check it against your definition of ready.
4. Commit to one action from your horizon calendar and one from your development map.

sections.heading: The thread, complete (running case)
sections.body:
| Horizon | Artefact |
|---|---|
| Strategy | On-time last-mile delivery 79% → ≥92% |
| Initiative | Product outcome: ≥70% of receivers confirm before route lock |
| Delivery | Story: receiver confirms window or safe drop via one-click link; value metric: % confirming within 4 hours |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

prompts.label: Final story with examples, criteria and NFRs

participant.aiPrompt: Review my elaborated backlog item below as a peer business analyst. Check that: examples include edge and unhappy cases; acceptance criteria derive from the examples and are observable; NFRs cover privacy, security, accessibility, performance and audit where relevant; the value metric is observable within days; and the trace to the strategic outcome is explicit. List the three most important improvements. Backlog item:

quiz.q: What closes the 'thread' across horizons?
opts: A trace from story value metric to strategic outcome
quiz.why: Traceability from story to outcome connects all three horizons.

quiz.q: Which item is part of a fully elaborated story in this course?
opts: Detailed UI mock-ups for all screens
Examples, criteria, NFRs and a value metric
quiz.why: These are the elements we defined for a fully elaborated item.

takeaways: You now have: an elaborated story, a horizon calendar and a development map.
Every story should trace to the strategic outcome.
Keep working across all three horizons.

presenter.purpose: Consolidate the final artefact, close the series thread and secure commitments.
presenter.openingLine: "Three days ago this was an 18-day wait. Let's finish by tracing your story all the way back."

beats.label: Brief
beats.notes: Explain steps.

beats.label: Individual work
beats.notes: Circulate; check traces.

beats.label: Commitments round
beats.notes: Everyone shares one commitment in chat; read a few aloud.

beats.label: Series close
beats.notes: Thank, point to resources, invite feedback survey.

presenter.facilitationNotes: End on time and on a high. Read the running-case thread table aloud as the final moment. Share the feedback survey link and the resources.
presenter.whatGood: A complete item and trace from every participant; specific commitments.
presenter.commonFailure: Running out of time — the fix: prioritise the trace and commitments over polishing examples.
debrief: What's your one commitment for next week?
What will you do differently at each horizon?
presenter.answerKey: Model trace as in section 2. Ready check: traces to hypothesis ✓; fits in iteration ✓; examples agreed ✓; dependencies (email service, middleware event) known ✓; criteria drafted ✓.
